results.title: Parameter Uncertainty - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Parameter uncertainty (PU) refers to uncertainty that arises from incomplete knowledge of model parameters or inputs due to insufficient or inaccurate data. Uncertainties in the parameters of a model are different from those of inputs. As discussed in this section, MPU could exist as uncertainty in the distribution of input parameters or uncertain parameters in a metamodel due to lack of sampling or inaccurate measurement. Moreover, the conclusion of some former studies indicating that the results of biofuel LC studies were largely dependent on the allocation method selected for co-product evaluation can be questioned when parameter uncertainty is included in the assessment, as recently demonstrated by Malça and Freire [10] for the production of vegetable oil from rapeseed in Europe. In case of epistemic uncertainty one can devise alternative scenarios, models, or parameter values; one can put alternative possibilities in a logic tree and assign probabilities, or rather weights, or even probability distributions to the possibilities and derive an overall probability distribution of outcomes performing a type of sensitivity analysis. Also, uncertainty can be defined quantitatively and qualitatively: the former is a measure which determines the spread of values attributed to a parameter while the latter refers to the lack of precision in data and methodologies due to incomplete data, lack of transparency, unrepresentative methods and the choice made [70]. : Stochastic modelling – to propagate uncertainty due to inaccurate data [188], input and output parameter uncertainty [184] and model uncertainty [101]. A probability distribution is generated by applying stochastic modelling, i.e. select a prior distribution type of uncertainties and employ Monte Carlo to calculate the indicator results of an impact category repeatedly. : Scenario comparison [101,186,187] – to investigate the effect of data and model uncertainties on the results via parameter variation (also known as scenario analysis). UFs are used to characterise the parameter uncertainty of input data while stochastic modelling (i.e. Monte Carlo or Latin Hypercube simulation) is applied to quantify and propagate parameter uncertainty of the output variables into a particular distribution type. In short, scientific approach by more research directly reduces uncertainties; scenario comparison and graphical approaches show the effects of inputs (e.g. parameters and choice) on the results; stochastic modelling, scale of uncertainties and UFs deal with uncertainties while analytical method, fuzzy number, Bayesian and hybrid LCI by nature propagate uncertainties.

results.title: Uncertainty Analysis for Computer Simulations through Validation and Calibration
results.content: ## Uncertainty Analysis for Computer Simulations through Validation and Calibration. ##### Files. McFarlandDissertation.pdf (3.03 MB). ##### Date. ##### Authors. ##### Journal Title. ##### Journal ISSN. ##### Volume Title. ##### Publisher. ##### Abstract. Modeling and simulation have played an increasingly important role in the design and analysis of engineering systems. High-consequence decisions are often informed strongly by numerical results obtained through the use of computational simulations, such as finite element models. This work is concerned with the development and improvement of methods that support the quantification of the uncertainty associated with predictions obtained using computer simulations. One avenue for addressing this uncertainty is the process known as model validation, which is concerned with comparing simulation predictions with experimentally observed outcomes for the purpose of developing confidence in the simulation model. One objective of this dissertation is to develop a better understanding of how quantitative statistical decision making tools can be better used to support the validation process. The primary focus of this dissertation, however, is to explore how the uncertainty associated with model predictions can be addressed by quantifying uncertainty associated with estimated parameters. Virtually all large-scale computer simulations possess some input parameters that are not directly observable (and may not even represent physical quantities) and must be estimated using experimental data. The process of estimating these inputs is typically referred to as model calibration, because it involves adjusting the unknown inputs in order to improve the agreement between the model output and available data. This dissertation shows that by quantifying the uncertainty in estimated calibration parameters in a meaningful way, this uncertainty can then be propagated through the computer simulation in order to quantify the resulting uncertainty associated with new predictions made using the computer simulation. Bayesian inference and Gaussian process surrogate modeling techniques are employed to develop comprehensive representations of uncertainty for expensive simulations. Other practical considerations are addressed as well, such as the use of surrogate modeling techniques to develop approximations to simulation models with highly multivariate (e.g., time series) output. ##### Description. ##### Keywords. model calibration, model validation, bayesian statistics, surrogate modeling, Gaussian processes, Uncertainty (Information theory) -- Mathematical models, Computer simulation -- Evaluation, Computer programs -- Validation.

results.title: Bayesian calibration and uncertainty quantification for a large nutrient load impact model - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Bayesian calibration and uncertainty quantification for a large nutrient load impact model. We propose an algorithm for quantifying uncertainties in a large nutrient impact model. We solve posterior distribution for biological parameters of a nutrient impact model. We propagate parameter uncertainty into nutrient load reduction scenario predictions. In this work, we developed a novel Bayesian computational approach for estimating the uncertainties in predictions of the Finnish coastal nutrient load model FICOS. After that, we constructed a space-filling design for FICOS model runs around the posterior mode and used it to train a Gaussian process emulator for the (log) posterior density of the model parameters. We then integrated over this (approximate) parameter posterior to produce probabilistic predictions for algal biomass and chlorophyll concentration under alternative nutrient load reduction scenarios. The posterior predictive scenarios showed that the probability to reach the EU’s Water Framework Directive objectives in the Finnish Archipelago Sea is generally low even under large load reductions.

results.title: 133. What is Uncertainty Quantification? | by Ilakkuvaselvi (Ilak) Manoharan | Medium
results.content: 3 min readFeb 28, 2024 * Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is a branch of applied mathematics and computational science that deals with the study, characterization, and management of uncertainties in mathematical models and simulations. * The primary goal of uncertainty quantification is to provide quantitative measures of uncertainty associated with predictions, simulations, or model outputs. * It aims to enhance decision-making processes by providing insights into the reliability and robustness of model predictions in the presence of uncertainty. * Sources of Uncertainty: Uncertainties in mathematical models can arise from various sources, including variability in input parameters, measurement errors, model simplifications, and incomplete knowledge about underlying physical processes. * Propagation of Uncertainty: UQ involves propagating uncertainties from input parameters through mathematical models or simulations to estimate their impact on output variables of interest. * Characterization and Representation: Uncertainties are characterized and represented using probability distributions, statistical measures (e.g., mean, variance), or probabilistic models. * Validation and Verification: UQ techniques often involve validation and verification processes to assess the accuracy and reliability of computational models in predicting real-world phenomena under uncertain conditions. * Monte Carlo Simulation: Generates random samples from input parameter distributions to estimate statistical properties of model outputs through repeated simulations. * Response Surface Modeling: Constructs surrogate models to approximate the relationship between input parameters and model outputs, facilitating efficient uncertainty analysis and sensitivity studies. * Global Sensitivity Analysis: Analyzes the relative importance of input parameters in contributing to output uncertainty and variability, aiding in model calibration and refinement. * Environmental Modeling: UQ techniques help quantify uncertainties in environmental models used for climate prediction, air quality assessment, and natural hazard mitigation. * Healthcare and Pharmaceuticals: UQ is employed in pharmacokinetic modeling, clinical trials, and epidemiological studies to evaluate the uncertainty in drug efficacy, disease spread, and treatment outcomes. * Computational Complexity: UQ techniques often involve computationally intensive simulations, particularly for high-dimensional or complex models, posing challenges in terms of scalability and efficiency. * Model Formulation and Calibration: Properly characterizing uncertainties and selecting appropriate probability distributions for input parameters require careful consideration and validation of model assumptions. * Data Availability and Quality: UQ relies on observational data or experimental measurements to calibrate and validate models, highlighting the importance of data quality, quantity, and representativeness.

How did high-dimensional quasi Monte Carlo methods advance uncertainty quantification? "Traditional" methods, such as standard Monte Carlo and Latin Hypercube Sampling, for propagating uncertainty and developing probability densities of model outputs, may in fact require performing a prohibitive number of model simulations. This is accomplished by approximating both inputs and outputs of the uncertain system through stochastic series of "well behaved" standard random variables; the series expansions of the outputs contain unknown coefficients which are calculated by a method that uses the results of a limited number of model simulations. The results obtained agree closely with those of traditional Monte Carlo and Latin Hypercube Sampling methods, while significantly reducing the required number of model simulations. Here, we present an innovative Bayesian method, called Conditional Robust Calibration (CRC), for nonlinear model calibration and robustness analysis using omics data. We apply CRC to three Ordinary Differential Equations (ODE) models to test its performances compared to the other state of the art approaches, namely Profile Likelihood (PL), Approximate Bayesian Computation Sequential Monte Carlo (ABC-SMC), and Delayed Rejection Adaptive Metropolis (DRAM).
